title: A Framework for Managing the Models of Engineered Quantum Systems
authors: Siyuan Ji, Hayato Ishida, Amal Elsokary, Stephen Powley, Catherine White, Alexandre Zagoskin, Ran Wei, Maria Aslam, Michael J. de C. Henshaw
abstract: Quantum technologies are maturing into systems that classical engineering must build, verify and maintain. The model-driven community has begun to respond with quantum-aware pipelines and languages, and the domain models these produce must be synchronised with the heterogeneous models created and owned by other communities. We argue that existing synchronisation approaches are insufficient for engineered quantum systems. A quantum system description captures superposition and entanglement, which a model transformation could remove undetected, while every structural check passes. To address this, we present the Quantum Systems Model Management (QSysMM) Framework, which guides the construction and synchronisation of the models of a quantum system into a digital single source of truth. The framework features four concerns: ontological, abstraction, composition and exposure, each given the treatment that engineered quantum systems require. Within this framework, we propose a Quantum Systems Modelling Language (QSysML) on the SysML v2 technology stack, and we close with a proposal that matures this synchronisation core into full model management for quantum systems.
summary: This paper introduces the Quantum Systems Model Management (QSysMM) Framework to solve the problem of maintaining consistency across heterogeneous models describing engineered quantum systems. It argues that standard model synchronization fails because it cannot track the loss of quantum information like entanglement during abstraction. The framework formalizes this management using four concerns and proposes a language, QSysML, to enforce physical admissibility checks throughout the modeling lifecycle.
main_problem: Existing model synchronization approaches are insufficient for engineered quantum systems because standard transformations can discard crucial quantum content like superposition and entanglement while structural checks remain valid.
main_result: The paper proposes the Quantum Systems Model Management (QSysMM) Framework to guide the construction and synchronization of quantum system models into a digital single source of truth.
method: It introduces QSysML, built on SysML v2, which structures model management around four concerns: ontological, abstraction, composition, and exposure, enforcing physical admissibility checks during transformations.
model_or_system: The framework addresses heterogeneous models describing engineered quantum systems, such as superconducting transmon qubits, integrating inputs from physics (Hamiltonians), engineering specs ($T_1, T_2$), software (Qiskit objects), and systems control layers.
key_observables: Consistency across domain boundaries; tracing physical properties back to the underlying physics; failure rates under different noise assumptions.
important_parameters: Superposition, entanglement, $T_1 = 50 \mu s$, $T_2 = 30 \mu s$, drive frequency (e.g., $5.2 	ext{ GHz}$), error rate thresholds ($< 10^{-3}$).
main_assumptions: Standard structural checks are insufficient for quantum consistency; the framework must enforce physical admissibility beyond mere structural compatibility.
figures_summary: Figure 1 depicts the QSysMM Framework structure, showing how the four concerns (Ontological, Abstraction, Composition, Exposure) interact to form consistent viewpoints over a federated model. Table 1 illustrates descriptions of a transmon qubit from multiple semantic domains.
paper_structure: The paper identifies the failure modes of current synchronization methods for quantum systems and then details the QSysMM framework, defining its four core concerns (Ontological, Abstraction, Composition, Exposure) and proposing QSysML as its implementation language.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, model-theoretic approach to managing complexity in quantum hardware development by formalizing how physical constraints must govern software/engineering abstractions, which is crucial for scaling up quantum devices.
